I keep getting stuck on that same point too. When you see real, visible suffering, it feels wrong to do nothing. But then the question is, does the mandate actually help if it's forced by a system people don't trust? It might just cause more resistance and chaos, even if the tool itself works.

You summed up my exact feeling. The mandate becomes the point of control. I keep thinking of the kids in the hospital, but if the whole thing is built to manufacture consent, then going along with it feels like you're enabling the corruption, not solving the problem.

GlacierWalk, I get that in a real outbreak, inaction has costs. But if the system defining 'outbreak' is corrupted, how do we know it's real? Using a flawed tool might just enforce a manufactured crisis.

Yeah, that's it exactly. It's like we're all agreeing the tool could technically work, but the operating manual is written in a language nobody trusts. So we just keep ending up back at 'fix the system first' and the debate goes nowhere.

That's it, exactly. You can have the clearest, most obvious crisis imaginable, but if the response is dictated by the same broken pipeline, the mandate just becomes an arm of that system. So even if the *idea* of a mandate isn't inherently wrong, in practice it's just not a tool we can use right now.

That's the part I find completely disqualifying. When the data pipeline itself is a control point, you can never get to an honest 'public health' decision. It means any mandate is built on a foundation that's already been shaped by the interests pushing it. That's why I'm stuck opposing them, even if the underlying idea of stopping an outbreak makes sense in theory.

I think that's where I'm stuck too. The logic seems to lead to a dead end. Until the structural conflict of interest is genuinely removed, I can't see a path to trusting a government mandate, even as a theoretical last resort. The trust has to come first, and right now, I don't see it.
